# MANIFOLDS WITH WEAKLY REDUCIBLE GENUS-THREE TRISECTIONS ARE STANDARD

Theorem 1.3. Suppose X admits a weakly reducible genus-three trisection T. Then either T is reducible, or T contains a five-chain. In particular, X is diffeomorphic to a spun lens space Sp or its sibling Sp, S4, or a connected sum of copies of CP?, S' × S%, and S2 × S2.

A trisection T is determined up to diffeomorphism by its spine, the union of three

3-dimensional handlebodies Ho U HgU H. A trisection T is said to be reducible if there is a curve e bounding disks in all three handlebodies; in this case, we can split T into a connected sum of smaller-genus trisections. In a foundational result from Heegaard theory, Casson and Gordon proved that if a 3-manifold Y admits a weakly reducible Heegaard splitting, then either the splitting is reducible or Y contains an essential surface [CG87]- We adapt weak reducibility to the setting of trisections, providing further evidence that key ideas from Heegaard theory can inform new insights in dimension four via trisections. We say that T is weakly reducible if there are disjoint non-separating curves e and c' such that e bounds a disk in one of the three handlebodies, and e bounds a disk in the other two.

See [ST94] for additional discussion of weak reduction in the context of Heegaard splittings.

A fice-chain is a specific sequence of five curves bounding disks in each of the three handlebodies such that consecutive curves intersect once and other pairs of curves are disjoint. A more rigorous definition can be found in Section à, in which we show that if T admits a five-chain, then X can be obtained by surgery on a loop & in a manifold X' admitting a lower-genus trisection T'. The proof of Theorem 1.3 relies heavily on ideas from the theory of Heegaard splittings and uses a variety of tools and techniques, including connections between 4-manifolds and Dehn surgery on knots in 3-manifolds, weak reduction and thin position of Heegaard splittings, and many ideas arising in the proof of Theorem 1.1- In the spirit of classifying as many genus-three trisections as possible, we prove a stronger version of Theorem 1.3 using the same techniques. Theorem 1.4. Suppose a genus-three trisection T of X admits a dependent triple. Then either T is reducible, or T contains a five-chain. In particular, X is diffcomorphic to a spun lens space Sp or its sibling Sp, S", or a connected sum of copies of +CP?, S' × S3, and S2 x S2.

Corollary 1.5. If X is simply-connected and admits a genus-three trisection T with a dependent triple, then X is diffeomorphic to S* or a connected sum of copies of ICE, and S° × S.

Corollary 1.5 is notable in light of the trisection genus additivity problem, which asks whether g(X1# X2) - 9(X1) + g(X2). In particular, there are examples of exotic CF2 #°CP- (manifolds X homcomorphic but not diffcomorphie to CP? #?CT) [AP10, FS11]. If trisection genus is additive, then the fact that there is some & such that X#$(52 × S2) is diffcomorphic to CF2#2CF #*(S × 52) [Wal64] implics that g(X) = g(CB2#2CF) = 3.
